tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

# AREA 7 — TOML Reading/Writing Specification for `pier` 0.1.6

All tests run with `HOME=/tmp/probe_1077`, `PIER_CONFIG_PATH` pointed at sandbox files. The binary behaves exactly like a Rust tool using the `toml` 0.4/0.5-era crate (serde derive) — both the parser error strings and the serializer's string-representation logic match it.

## 1. Data model (deduced from serde errors + write oracle)

Config struct:
- `scripts`: map alias → Script. Required... actually optional: a config with no `[scripts]` parses fine.
- `default`: struct, optional; written even when absent from source.

Script struct fields (in serialization order): `command` (String, **required**), `description` (Option<String>), `reference` (Option<String>), `tags` (Vec<String>, defaults to empty; omitted from output when absent... see §4). An `alias` key inside a script table is **ignored** (dropped on write).

`[default]` struct fields (serialization order): `interpreter` (Option<Vec<String>>), `command_width` (Option<usize>). Only these two are recognized; all other keys are silently dropped on write. Default `command_width` when unset = **80** (verified: 81-char command truncated to 80 in `list`, 80-char not truncated). `interpreter` is used as the shell for `run` (default effectively `["sh","-c"]`, not verified further — outside area).

Unknown keys anywhere (top-level, `[scripts.x]`, `[default]`, unknown sections) are **accepted on parse and silently discarded on write**. Even *duplicate* unknown keys are accepted (`zzz = 1` + `zzz = 2` → exit 0).

## 2. `config-init` output (exact bytes)

```
[scripts.hello-pier]
command = 'echo Hello, Pier!'
description = 'This is an example command.'

[default]
```
File ends with `]\n` after `[default]` (no trailing blank line). `config-init` on an existing path: exit 1, stderr `error: Cannot initialize config at <path>, file already exists.\n`, file untouched. New file created with mode 0666 & ~umask. `add` etc. rewrite the file **in place** (existing permissions preserved, e.g. 600 stayed 600).

## 3. WRITE serialization rules (identical for add/remove/move/copy/edit)

General layout:
- Scripts emitted as `[scripts.ALIAS]` tables, sorted by alias in **byte order** (observed: `1num` < `A` < `Z` < `a` < `b` < `hello-pier` < `héllo`; also `with space` < `with"dquote` < `with'quote` < `with=eq`).
- Exactly one blank line between tables; file starts directly with the first `[scripts.x]` line; then one blank line, then `[default]` **always last**, even if source had it first or absent. File always ends with a single `\n`, no trailing blank line.
- Key order within a script always: `command`, `description`, `reference`, `tags` — present-only-if-set, except `command` always present. `tags` present iff the parsed script had tags (an explicit `tags = []` round-trips as `tags = []`; never added by `add` without `-t`). `description = ''` round-trips (empty string is written, not omitted). `-d ""` writes `description = ''`.
- With zero scripts (after removing the last one): file is exactly `[scripts]\n\n[default]\n`.
- Key order within `[default]`: `interpreter` then `command_width`, regardless of source order; each omitted when unset.
- Everything is re-serialized from the parsed model: comments, original quoting style, key order, inline tables, unknown keys/sections — all lost.

Key (alias) encoding:
- Bare if it matches `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` (incl. pure digits like `123`), else a basic-quoted key `"..."` with `"` → `\"`, `\t` → `\t`, `\n` → `\n` etc. Dots do NOT create nesting: alias `a.b` written as `[scripts."a.b"]`.
- Non-ASCII aliases are quoted (`[scripts."héllo"]`).
- BUG: empty alias (`add -a '' ...`) is accepted, prints `Added \n`, writes `[scripts.]` — which pier itself cannot parse afterwards.

Array formatting (tags and interpreter):
- 0 elements: `[]`; 1 element: inline `['x']` (no spaces inside brackets, even for very long elements).
- ≥2 elements: multiline, 4-space indent, trailing comma:
  ```
  tags = [
      'tag1',
      'tag2',

  ```
- Tag order preserved as given on CLI (not sorted).

String encoding decision tree (empirically mapped; matches toml-rs 0.5 `emit_str`):

Let PRETTY-OK = string contains no `'` run of ≥3, does not end with `'`, and contains no control chars < 0x20 **except** `\t` and `\n` (note: U+007F is treated as allowed — see bugs). "clean-basic" = contains no `"`, no `\`, and no control chars < 0x20 **including** `\t`.

1. No `\n` in string:
   - If no `'` and PRETTY-OK → single-line literal: `'s'` (raw tab, raw `"`, raw `\`, raw UTF-8, raw `\x7f` allowed).
   - Else if clean-basic → single-line basic: `"s"` (so `'`-containing strings with no `"`/`\\`/tab/control go here, incl. strings ending in `'` or containing `'''`).
   - Else if PRETTY-OK → oneline triple literal: `'''s'''` (used e.g. for strings containing both `'` and `"`, or `'` plus tab).
   - Else → single-line basic with escapes.
2. Contains `\n`:
   - If PRETTY-OK → `'''` + `\n` + raw content + `'''` (leading newline after opening delimiter always present; raw newlines, raw `'`, raw `"`, raw tab).
   - Else → `"""` + `\n` + content + `"""` with escapes: every `"` → `\"` (even lone ones mid-string), `\` → `\\`, control chars escaped, newlines raw. (Used when content ends with `'`, contains `'''`, or has control chars.)

Escape table (basic strings): `\b`→`\b`, `\t`→`\t`, `\f`→`\f`, `\r`→`\r`, `"`→`\"`, `\`→`\\`, other C0 controls → `\u00XX` (4 lowercase hex digits, e.g. `\u0001`). `\n` is never escaped (its presence forces multiline form, where it's raw). Non-ASCII written as raw UTF-8.

SERIALIZER/PARSER MISMATCH BUG: U+007F (DEL) is **never escaped** by the serializer — written raw into literal or basic strings — but the parser rejects it: `invalid character in string: `\u{7f}` at line N`. Any string containing `\x7f` bricks the config after the next write. (Same class of bug as the empty-alias `[scripts.]` case.)

## 4. READ parsing behavior

Parser is standard TOML (toml-rs): accepts comments, all string forms, multiline strings with `\` line continuation, `\uXXXX`/`\UXXXXXXXX` escapes, inline tables (`scripts = {a = {command = "x"}}` and `[scripts]` + `a = {command="x"}` both work), dotted keys (`[scripts]` + `a.command = "x"` works → alias `a`), hex ints, `inf`, datetimes, `1_000` (for unknown keys), CRLF line endings, UTF-8 BOM (silently skipped), missing trailing newline. Quoted dotted alias `[scripts."a.b"]` → single alias `a.b`. Unquoted `[scripts.a.b]` → nested map → serde error.

Read-only commands (`list`, `show`) never modify the file (md5 verified).

## 6. Round-trip fidelity summary

Hand-written exotic config (comments, swapped key order, inline arrays, unknown keys/sections, `[default]` extras) parses fine, but any mutating command rewrites it to canonical form: sorted `[scripts.x]` tables, fixed key order (`command`, `description`, `reference`, `tags`), literal-quote-preferred strings, arrays inline if ≤1 element else multiline 4-space/trailing-comma, `[default]` last containing only `interpreter`/`command_width` (in that order) — everything else (comments, unknown sections like `[other_section]`, unknown keys, original formatting) destroyed. A hand-written `description = ""` becomes `description = ''`; `tags = []` stays `[]`.

Ambiguities not fully pinned down: the exact internal predicate order of the string-representation choice is empirical (all observed cases consistent with §3, but an untested combination could in theory reveal a different tie-break); whether `interpreter` default is literally `["sh","-c"]` wasn't verified (outside TOML area).
